The scope is also limited to direct API usage. The announcement does not change the experience of regular ChatGPT app users, whose requests are not covered by the new arrangement. The change concerns businesses and developers who call OpenAI models through the API and who require processing to remain inside the country.

## Why India, and why now

The announcement is aimed at data-localisation requirements, the rules and policies under which certain kinds of data must be processed and stored within a country's borders. Financial services firms are named in the reporting as a category of customer for which such requirements are particularly strict, because regulators in the sector commonly require sensitive data to remain inside the jurisdiction. Nitin Bawankule, Head of Enterprise for India at OpenAI, was named in the coverage as the executive associated with the announcement.

India is one of the largest markets for OpenAI by user numbers, and the company has been expanding its presence there through the "OpenAI for India" initiative. The Tata Group data-centre partnership, cited as background in the reporting, is part of that expansion. The reports do not state whether the in-country processing announced on 12 November runs on infrastructure built under that partnership.

## Why it matters

For Indian businesses subject to data-localisation rules, the difference between storage residency and inference residency is practical rather than technical. A company that stores data in India but sends it abroad for processing may still fall short of a requirement that the data remain within the country throughout its handling. Full in-country inference closes that gap for the workloads covered by the announcement, at least for customers who meet the stated conditions.

The conditions, however, narrow the benefit. A customer that relies on hosted tools, or that uses a model other than GPT-6 Luna, cannot yet use the regional processing capability. The requirement for Zero Data Retention and Standard pay-as-you-go processing may also exclude customers on other processing arrangements. The announcement therefore represents a defined first step rather than a general availability of in-country processing for all Indian API use.

## What to watch next

The reporting to date leaves several questions open. OpenAI has not disclosed a timetable for adding models beyond GPT-6 Luna to the India regional processing capability, nor for making hosted tools available for regional processing. It has not published a list of eligible customers or detailed criteria, and it has not stated whether capacity will expand to further markets.

The development is also likely to be measured against competitors. Other providers of frontier models have made their own data-residency commitments in regulated markets, and the value of OpenAI's announcement will depend in part on how quickly the conditions are relaxed and the model coverage widened. For now, the verifiable position is that GPT-6 Luna API workloads for eligible Indian customers can be processed and stored entirely in India, subject to Zero Data Retention and Standard pay-as-you-go processing, without hosted tools, through the India regional endpoint.

Sources: The Economic Times; The Times of India; The Hindu BusinessLine; PTI via Rediff; Express Computer. Reporting date: 12 November 2026.

title: Samsung breaks ground on ₩6 trillion HBM packaging fab as Chungcheong investment rises to ₩144 trillion
body:
Samsung Electronics held a groundbreaking ceremony on Thursday, 12 November 2026, for a new advanced semiconductor packaging facility at its Onyang Campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province. The facility, designated Onyang Line 5, represents an investment of ₩6 trillion (approximately $4.5 billion) and will produce next-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for artificial intelligence applications. Construction has been brought forward by approximately one year relative to the original schedule, and operations are targeted to begin in June 2028.

The ceremony also served as the occasion for Samsung to raise its total committed investment in the Chungcheong region to ₩144 trillion (approximately $108 billion), an increase of ₩4 trillion from the ₩140 trillion announced in July 2026. The commitment spans the group's principal affiliates and covers semiconductor packaging, displays, electronic components and batteries. A further ₩40 trillion in phased equipment investment is planned at the Onyang site, according to the reports of the ceremony.

## The Onyang Line 5 facility

The new plant is a three-storey facility with a footprint of approximately 31,000 square metres. It will house advanced packaging lines for next-generation HBM, the stacked memory used alongside AI accelerators in data centres. Packaging, the process of assembling and interconnecting memory dies into finished modules, has become a central stage of the AI memory supply chain, because the performance of HBM depends as much on the density and quality of the interconnections as on the memory cells themselves.

The decision to move construction forward by approximately one year indicates the urgency with which Samsung is approaching the AI memory market. The company has not disclosed a specific production capacity or a customer list for the new line. Operations are targeted for June 2028, a date that should be read as a company target rather than a confirmed start of mass production, since the ramp of a packaging line depends on equipment installation, qualification and customer orders that have not been publicly specified.

## A ₩144 trillion regional commitment

The raised regional commitment of ₩144 trillion is divided among four Samsung affiliates. Samsung Electronics accounts for ₩60 trillion, Samsung Display for ₩67 trillion, Samsung Electro-Mechanics for ₩8 trillion and Samsung SDI for ₩9 trillion. The figures are commitments announced by the group, not expenditure already incurred, and the reports do not give a single end date for the full programme.

The scale of the programme makes Chungcheong Province one of the largest single regional concentrations of Samsung investment. The additional ₩40 trillion in phased equipment investment at Onyang, announced alongside the groundbreaking, is separate from the ₩144 trillion total and will be spent over an unspecified period as the new packaging capacity is equipped.

## Display investment in Asan

The largest single share of the commitment belongs to Samsung Display, whose ₩67 trillion includes the A7 OLED production line in Asan. Construction of that line began in October 2026, and mass production is targeted for the second half of 2029. The A7 line is intended to produce OLED panels for information technology products, extending the display affiliate's production base in the region alongside Samsung Electronics' semiconductor operations.

The grouping of semiconductor packaging and OLED display capacity in the same province reflects the geographic concentration of Samsung's manufacturing. Asan already hosts Samsung Display's principal OLED production, and the Onyang campus is the group's established site for semiconductor packaging and testing.

## Attendance at the ceremony

President Lee Jae-myung attended the groundbreaking ceremony and spoke at the event, as did Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong. The presence of both the president and the group's chairman at a factory groundbreaking is a measure of the political and industrial weight attached to the investment, which the government has presented as part of South Korea's effort to hold its position in the global semiconductor supply chain.

Neither the government nor Samsung has disclosed further details of any public support attached to the project, and the reports of the ceremony do not specify whether the investment figures include government incentives.

## Why it matters

High-bandwidth memory is one of the most supply-constrained components in the AI hardware market. Demand for AI accelerators has raised demand for HBM faster than producers have been able to add capacity, and packaging capacity, rather than wafer fabrication alone, has become a bottleneck. A dedicated packaging facility at Onyang addresses that bottleneck directly, and the accelerated construction schedule suggests Samsung expects demand to remain strong through the end of the decade.

The broader ₩144 trillion commitment also signals that Samsung intends to compete across the full stack of AI-era hardware: memory packaging at Samsung Electronics, displays at Samsung Display, substrates and components at Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and batteries at Samsung SDI. Whether the programme delivers its stated investment on schedule will depend on demand for AI hardware, the pace of construction and equipment installation, and the group's own capital allocation in the years ahead.

## What is next

The immediate milestone is the construction of the three-storey plant at Onyang, with operations targeted for June 2028. The A7 OLED line in Asan is scheduled to reach mass production in the second half of 2029. The phased ₩40 trillion equipment investment at Onyang will follow as the packaging lines are fitted out. Further detail on capacity, customers and the timing of equipment spending has not been disclosed.

Sources: The Korea Herald; Seoul Economic Daily; The Herald Business — 12 November 2026.

title: Runway open-sources Praxis-1, a 27B robot brain anyone can run
body:
Runway has released the open weights of Praxis-1, a 27-billion-parameter robot model that predicts video and physical actions together, under the Apache 2.0 licence. The release, announced on 11 November 2026, makes the weights, inference code and fine-tuning code freely available for research and commercial use, with the model distributed through GitHub and Hugging Face and supported by the LeRobot robotics framework. The announcement follows a preview of the model in September 2026. The 11 November event is the open-weights release itself, not the first public announcement of the system.

## What Praxis-1 is

Praxis-1 is what Runway calls a world action model. It is a mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer with 27 billion parameters in total. Its video backbone contains 26.9 billion parameters, of which approximately 2.8 billion are active for each token, and it is paired with a 314-million-parameter action expert. The two components operate together: on each call, the model imagines the next 1.6 seconds of video and derives 24 action rows at 15 hertz from that prediction. In effect, the model plans motion by first predicting what the scene will look like and then reading robot commands from that prediction.

The model is intended for general-purpose robotic manipulation rather than a single task or a single robot. Runway published three checkpoints with the release: a base model, a single-arm model fine-tuned on the DROID dataset, and a bimanual model fine-tuned on the YAM dataset. The two fine-tuned checkpoints are intended to give developers working models for common arm configurations, while the base model provides a starting point for fine-tuning on new hardware and tasks.

## Benchmark results

According to Runway, Praxis-1 leads the RoboLab-120 leaderboard with a success rate of 46.2 percent, corresponding to 555 successful episodes out of 1,200. The nearest competitors on the same leaderboard are FLUX 3 Action at 42.9 percent, Cosmos3 Nano at 36.8 percent, and pi0.5 at 28.0 percent. These figures are Runway's own reported results and have not been independently reproduced. RoboLab-120 is a simulated benchmark consisting of 120 tabletop tasks, each run ten times. A 46.2 percent success rate therefore means the model fails in more than half of simulated attempts, and simulation performance is not a measure of reliability on physical hardware.

The benchmark result is nevertheless notable because it places an openly available model ahead of systems from larger, well-funded rivals on the same test. The comparison is limited to the RoboLab-120 task set, and Runway has not published equivalent results for other widely used manipulation benchmarks.

## Hardware and availability

Runway states that Praxis-1 runs across a range of hardware, from H100 and B200 data-centre GPUs to RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 workstations and to Jetson Thor modules mounted on the robot itself. The full model in bfloat16 precision occupies 54.4 gigabytes and requires a single GPU with 80 gigabytes of memory. The workstation and on-robot paths therefore depend on a quantised version rather than the full-precision model.

An experimental 4-bit NVFP4 quantised checkpoint occupies 17.5 gigabytes and is the version intended for RTX 5090-class hardware. Runway itself states that the speed and closed-loop accuracy of this quantised version still need measurement, so its real-time performance on consumer hardware remains unverified at the time of writing. Developers should treat the workstation claim as provisional until Runway or independent testers publish measured results.

Three launch partners are already running the model in their own systems: Noble Machines, Standard Bots and Ultra. Their involvement gives the release an immediate base of real-world deployments, although no performance figures from those deployments have been published.

## Known limitations

Runway's own report lists failure modes that developers should expect. The model struggles with look-alike objects, where two similar items are present in the scene; with vague instructions, where the task description does not specify enough detail; and with long single-prompt tasks, where a complex instruction is given as one prompt rather than broken into steps. These are characteristic weaknesses of vision-language-action models and are not unique to Praxis-1.

The open-weights licence is permissive: Apache 2.0 allows commercial use, modification and redistribution. The model is therefore available to any organisation that can meet the hardware requirements, including commercial robotics companies and academic laboratories.

## Why it matters

The release arrives in a year of rapid movement in robot foundation models. Google has advanced Gemini Robotics 2.5 and NVIDIA has advanced GR00T 2, both of which pursue the same goal of a general model for physical manipulation. Praxis-1 differs from those systems in that its weights are openly available under a permissive licence, while its competitors remain closed or partially restricted. Open weights lower the cost of entry for smaller robotics teams and make it possible to audit, fine-tune and extend the model without a commercial agreement.

The practical consequence is that a robotics team with an 80-gigabyte GPU can now run a model that, on one simulated benchmark, outperforms the leading alternatives. That is a meaningful shift in who can work at the frontier of robot learning. The caveat is equally clear: the benchmark is simulated, the success rate is below half, and the hardware requirements remain high. Open access does not remove those constraints; it makes them visible to a wider community that can now test and improve the model directly.

## What comes next

The next evidence to watch is measured performance of the quantised checkpoint on workstation hardware and results from the three launch partners' deployments. Independent reproduction of the RoboLab-120 figures, and results on physical robots rather than simulation, will determine whether the benchmark lead transfers to real-world manipulation. Runway has not disclosed a timetable for further checkpoints or for a quantised version with measured closed-loop accuracy.

Source: Runway official announcement; RobotsBeat; AI Frontier Post; AlphaSignal; The Robot Report.

title: Investors fear an Nvidia without Huang — $600B selloff as board decides his fate
body:
Nvidia has lost approximately 600 billion dollars in market value during the course of this week, a decline that has removed the company from its position as the most valuable listed company in the world and placed it second. The selloff accelerated on Wednesday after reports that the board of directors was preparing to remove Jensen Huang, the chief executive who has led the company since its founding and who is widely regarded as inseparable from its rise in artificial intelligence computing. The board met late on Wednesday. No decision was announced.

The scale of the decline is notable even by the standards of a stock that has experienced sharp swings during the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia shares have fallen approximately 11 percent over the last five trading days. On Wednesday, the shares fell approximately 8 percent in after-hours trading following the reports concerning the board. The movement reflects a specific anxiety among investors: that the company, and by extension the broader market for artificial intelligence hardware, may be difficult to value without the executive who built its dominant position.

## The market reaction

The decline has extended beyond Nvidia itself. CoreWeave, a data-centre operator backed by Nvidia, fell more than 6 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday. At the same time, shares of Chinese graphics processor makers rose sharply on Thursday. Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon each gained nearly 10 percent, a movement that suggests some investors expect a weakening of Nvidia to create space for competitors in markets where the company has faced export restrictions.

The reaction indicates that the market is treating the reports as material to the valuation of the company rather than as a governance matter of limited consequence. Nvidia is the central supplier of the accelerators on which large-scale artificial intelligence training depends, and its share price has become a proxy for confidence in the entire sector. A fall of approximately 600 billion dollars in market value in a single week is, by itself, larger than the total market capitalisation of most listed companies.

## The board meeting

According to the reports, the board met late on Wednesday to consider the future of Huang. No decision was announced following the meeting, and the company has not confirmed the substance of the deliberations. The absence of a statement leaves the position uncertain: the board may act, it may decline to act, or it may continue its deliberations. Investors are therefore pricing a possibility rather than a confirmed outcome.

Huang is 63 years old and has never named a successor. That fact is central to the anxiety in the market. In companies where a long-serving founder chief executive has become identified with the strategy of the business, the absence of a named successor is often treated as a governance weakness. In this case the weakness is amplified by the scale of Nvidia's market value and by the pace at which its core market is changing.

## The succession question

Two internal candidates have been identified in reporting as the leading successors. Ian Buck, an engineer who is credited as the architect of CUDA, the software platform on which Nvidia's dominance in artificial intelligence computing rests, is reported to be favoured for the permanent chief executive role. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer since 2013, is reported to be favoured by some board members as an interim chief executive. Kress is 59 years old.

The distinction between the two candidates is instructive. Buck represents continuity in the technical direction of the company, while Kress represents continuity in its financial management. Neither has been confirmed as a candidate by the company, and the reporting does not establish that the board has settled on either name. The existence of two names, however, indicates that the board has at least begun to consider the mechanics of a transition.

Prediction markets have moved sharply on the reports. Polymarket places an approximately 83 percent chance that Huang resigns or is removed by the end of 2026. That figure should be treated with caution: the trading volume on the contract is small, and odds derived from thin markets can move rapidly on limited information. The figure is nevertheless a measure of the prevailing expectation among those willing to trade on the outcome.

## Why the market is reacting

The market reaction reflects more than a reaction to a single board meeting. Nvidia's valuation rests on two assumptions: that demand for artificial intelligence accelerators will continue to grow, and that the company will retain its dominant share of that demand. Both assumptions are, in the view of investors, bound up with Huang. He has directed the company's shift from graphics processing to general-purpose computing, and then to artificial intelligence, over a period of more than three decades. The question the market is asking is whether that judgement can be institutionalised or whether it resides in one individual.

The rise in the shares of Chinese graphics processor makers adds a further dimension. If Nvidia were to lose its chief executive at a moment when export controls already constrain its access to the Chinese market, competitors in that market could gain ground more quickly. The gains of nearly 10 percent in Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon on Thursday are consistent with that reading, although they are also consistent with a broader rotation into Chinese technology shares.

## What comes next

The immediate focus is the board. No date has been given for a further statement, and the company has not indicated when a decision might be announced. The next scheduled event of substance is the quarterly earnings report on 17 November, at which the company will present its financial results and, in the usual course, take questions from analysts. If the board has not acted by then, the earnings call is likely to be dominated by questions about the chief executive.

For investors, the calculation is now a matter of probabilities. The share price has already fallen approximately 11 percent in five days, which suggests that a substantial part of the risk is already reflected in the valuation. Whether the decline continues will depend on what the board does next, on who succeeds Huang if he departs, and on whether the company can demonstrate that its position in artificial intelligence computing does not depend on a single individual. Until those questions are answered, the uncertainty is likely to persist.

Source: Reuters; The Statesman; Tech in Asia; CNBC-TV18.

title: ElevenLabs launches 13 products and upgrades
body:
ElevenLabs has announced 13 new products and upgrades at its New York Summit, held on 11 November 2026, in the most extensive single release in the company's history. The announcements span speech recognition, expressive voice synthesis, real-time conversational agents, a new workplace application, an expanded partnership with NVIDIA, and a partner ecosystem that now extends across 44 countries. Together, they indicate a deliberate shift from standalone voice tools toward an integrated platform for enterprise voice artificial intelligence.

## The announcement in context

ElevenLabs, founded in 2022, has built its reputation on synthetic voice technology, with its text-to-speech and voice-cloning products adopted across media, publishing, and customer service. The New York Summit announcements arrive at a moment of intensifying competition among voice AI providers, as enterprises increasingly deploy conversational agents in customer-facing roles and as speech-to-text accuracy becomes a differentiating factor in regulated industries such as healthcare and financial services. The scale of this release, 13 products and upgrades presented in a single event, reflects the company's attempt to address that entire stack at once rather than incrementally.

## Three new voice models

The core of the release consists of three voice models shipped within the last month. Scribe v3 is the company's newest speech-to-text model, supporting transcription in 102 languages. According to ElevenLabs' own evaluation, Scribe v3 makes 27 percent fewer word errors than its predecessor, Scribe v2, across those 102 languages. That figure is the company's own testing and has not been independently verified. A healthcare-tuned variant, Scribe v3 Medical, has also launched, and Scribe v3 Live, a real-time transcription product, launched on 10 November 2026, one day before the Summit.

Eleven v4 is the company's newest expressive text-to-speech model, designed to produce speech with greater control over tone, pacing, and emotional register. Eleven Realtime, the third model, enables speech-to-speech conversational agents that listen and respond without an intermediate text stage, reducing latency in live interactions. The three models are positioned as complementary: Scribe v3 captures spoken input, Eleven Realtime sustains the conversation, and Eleven v4 renders the agent's spoken output.

## ElevenAI enters free early access

The most prominent product announcement is ElevenAI, a workplace application that converts spoken meetings into written notes, summaries, and action items. ElevenAI opened in free early access on 11 November 2026. The distinction matters: the product is available for early testing at no cost, but it has not reached a general commercial launch, and its feature set and pricing for a full release remain undisclosed.

ElevenAI places ElevenLabs in direct competition with established meeting transcription and summarisation tools. Its stated advantage is the integration of the company's own speech models, including Scribe v3, with agentic capabilities that can identify decisions and follow-up tasks from a conversation rather than merely transcribing it. Whether that integration produces measurably better meeting records than incumbent tools will depend on evidence from real-world use, which is not yet available.

## Expanded collaboration with NVIDIA

ElevenLabs also announced an expanded relationship with NVIDIA. The chipmaker's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model is now available within ElevenAgents, the company's platform for building voice agents. In addition, ElevenLabs plans to add 15 megawatts of NVIDIA Vera Rubin compute capacity. That capacity is planned, not yet live, and no deployment date has been disclosed. The announcement signals growing infrastructure investment, but the compute expansion should be read as a stated intention rather than an operational fact.

## A partner ecosystem across 44 countries

The company's Partner Program now counts more than 550 partners across 44 countries. ElevenLabs announced an alliance with McKinsey, working with the consultancy's QuantumBlack AI practice, and introduced a Marketplace through which more than 20 partners offer industry-specific applications built on ElevenLabs technology. Purchases through the Marketplace will be possible through customers' existing commitments only from 2027, a detail that limits its near-term commercial effect.

The partner figures describe the breadth of the ecosystem rather than its depth. ElevenLabs has not disclosed revenue attributable to partners, nor the number of partners actively deploying production systems, so the commercial significance of the 550-partner figure cannot be assessed from the announcement alone.

## What remains in preview

Several announced capabilities are not yet available. The Interaction Engine, a system for more natural conversational behaviour, was previewed rather than released. Memory, Routines, and Architect, features intended to give agents persistent context and structured workflows, were likewise presented as forthcoming. Enterprise fine-tuning is limited to selected enterprises and is expected to arrive in the coming months, while a financial-services model remains in development only. These items should be understood as a product roadmap, not as shipping software.

## Why the release matters

The announcement is significant for three reasons. First, the simultaneous release of recognition, synthesis, and real-time conversation models gives ElevenLabs a complete voice stack under one roof, reducing its dependence on third-party components. Second, ElevenAI moves the company from developer infrastructure into end-user workplace software, a larger and more contested market. Third, the NVIDIA collaboration and the McKinsey alliance suggest the company is positioning itself for enterprise deployments where infrastructure scale and consulting distribution matter as much as model quality.

At the same time, the release leaves important questions unanswered. The accuracy improvement claimed for Scribe v3 rests on the company's own evaluation, and no independent benchmark has been published. The 15-megawatt compute expansion has no timeline. The Marketplace will not support purchases through existing commitments until 2027. These gaps do not diminish the announcements, but they define the limits of what can presently be concluded about them.

## What to watch next

The immediate test for ElevenLabs is whether ElevenAI gains traction during its free early access period and whether the company converts that usage into paying customers. A second test is the delivery schedule for the previewed capabilities, particularly enterprise fine-tuning and the financial-services model, where regulated customers will require evidence of accuracy and compliance before deployment. A third is whether the planned NVIDIA compute capacity materialises on a disclosed timeline. Each of these will provide a clearer measure of the release than the announcement itself.

Source: Mumbrella; CIOL; Unite.AI.

title: Google launches Gemini Decisions API
body:
Google has introduced the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint built on a dedicated model, Gemini Decision 1, that evaluates up to 1,000 independent questions in a single request against one shared multimodal input. The announcement was made on November 11, 2026, by Min Choi and Felix Yu of Google DeepMind on the Google Developers Blog. The release arrives weeks after OpenAI introduced its own Decisions API last month, according to SiliconANGLE, and it marks a further step in the competition between the two companies to supply the decision-making layer for agent-based software.

## What the API does

The Gemini Decisions API is designed for a task that traditional language models handle inefficiently: answering many small, structured questions about the same input. A single request can carry text, images, audio, video, or PDF documents, up to 256,000 tokens of shared context, and can pose as many as 1,000 independent questions against that input. The questions fall into three types: yes or no, multiple choice with between 2 and 255 options, and rubric scoring.

Rather than generating each answer token by token, the model scores all questions in a single forward pass and returns probabilities together with confidence scores between 0 and 1 for each answer. The design removes the sequential decoding that makes a conventional model slow and expensive when the same document must be read once for each of many questions. According to Google, the shared input is billed once per request, and there are no charges for thinking tokens, optical character recognition, or transcription.

## Performance and pricing

Google reports end-to-end latency of 150 to 250 milliseconds, with median model compute of 50 to 100 milliseconds, measured at contexts of up to 16,000 tokens. Latency remains nearly flat as the number of questions rises from 1 to 100 per request. The company has not published equivalent latency figures for the maximum of 1,000 questions or for the full 256,000-token context, and no such claim should be inferred from the figures above.

Pricing is set at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens, with no charge for output tokens. Google states that the service is nearly five times cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite used with the Interactions API for comparable workloads. A no-cost tier is available in Google AI Studio for prototyping.

On benchmarks, Google reports that Gemini Decision 1 leads across its own evaluation suite with the lowest calibration error, a measure of how closely a model's stated confidence matches its actual accuracy. SiliconANGLE reports that the model outperforms Jev and OpenAI's Decisions API on seven of nine benchmarks in Google's comparison. These are Google's own claims, published by the company and reported by the outlet, rather than independently verified results.

## Where the model is already in use

Google describes several internal deployments. Gemini Notebook uses the model as a real-time router, and the company reports up to 40 percent lower latency on everyday queries as a result. Stitch, the company's interface-design tool, uses it for rapid canvas evaluation. The CC emoji picker relies on it to select among more than 200 options, and a Google Search safety layer uses it to assess Model Context Protocol tools.

The use cases Google names for developers are tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. Each of these is a task in which an application must make many small judgements quickly, and where the cost of a full generative response for every judgement would be prohibitive. A policy check, for example, may require dozens of separate yes-or-no determinations about a single document. A routing decision may require scoring every available tool or model against one request. In both cases, the value of the new endpoint lies in the combination of structured output, calibrated confidence, and low latency.

## Background and context

The release follows the pattern established by OpenAI's Decisions API, which launched last month. Both products address the same observation: as agent systems grow more capable, a large share of their work consists of classification and selection rather than open-ended generation. Dedicated scoring models are the natural response, and the two companies are now competing directly on price, latency, and calibration quality in this category.

The timing also reflects the broader direction of Google's Gemini programme. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, the company's efficient general-purpose model, remains the reference point for the pricing comparison, which suggests that Google positions the new endpoint as a complement to its general models rather than a replacement. The Decisions API handles the judgement calls; the general models handle the generation that follows from them.

## Why it matters

For developers building agent systems, the practical significance of the release is economic as much as technical. Scoring 1,000 questions against one input in a single pass, with the input billed once, changes the cost structure of applications that previously had to choose between reading a document once and asking one question, or paying to read it many times. The confidence scores add a second dimension: an application can act on high-confidence answers automatically and route low-confidence cases to a larger model or to a human reviewer.

The calibration claim is the most consequential part of the announcement, if it holds up in independent testing. A model that knows when it is uncertain is more useful in production than a model that is marginally more accurate but poorly calibrated, because the confidence score determines how much of the workflow can be automated safely. Google's claim of the lowest calibration error in its suite is therefore the figure that independent evaluation should examine first.

## Availability and what comes next

The Gemini Decisions API is available now through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, on the v1beta endpoint, using the model identifier gemini-decision-1. Support in Google Cloud is coming soon and is not yet live.

The next questions for the product are straightforward. Independent benchmarks will test whether the calibration and cost claims survive outside Google's own evaluation suite. Developers will determine whether the three question types cover the judgement tasks their applications require, or whether the format needs to expand. And the competitive response from OpenAI, which introduced the category only last month, will show how quickly this new class of model becomes a commodity. For now, Google has set the terms of the comparison: up to 1,000 questions, one shared input, and a price of $0.10 per 1 million tokens.

Source: Google Developers Blog / SiliconANGLE

title: Gemini finally drives onto Apple CarPlay
body:
Google has extended its Gemini assistant to Apple CarPlay as a standalone application, completing a rollout that began on November 11, 2026. The launch places Gemini on the in-car display of iPhone users worldwide, allowing drivers to hold spoken conversations with the assistant without handling their phone.

The release is significant because it changes how Gemini reaches the car. Until now, the assistant was available inside CarPlay only through Google Maps, an integration that arrived on October 21. With this update, Gemini gains its own app icon on the CarPlay home screen, and users can open it directly, independent of any navigation session.

## What changed

The standalone CarPlay app gives drivers access to Gemini Live, the voice mode of the assistant, from the car display. A driver can start a new conversation or resume a recent one by voice, and the assistant responds through the car's speakers. The interaction is designed to be hands-free: the driver speaks, Gemini answers, and no typing or phone handling is required while the vehicle is in motion.

According to Google, the rollout is global and covers all Gemini users on iOS, in every language in which Gemini Live is supported. The company did not publish a country-by-country schedule or a completion date, and no subscriber tier was named as a precondition. The rollout is staged, so availability reaches individual users as the update propagates rather than appearing for every user at the same moment.

## Requirements for drivers

Three conditions apply before the CarPlay app can be used. The iPhone must run the latest version of the Gemini app. Microphone permission for the app must be enabled. And the user must have used Gemini Live on the phone at least once before the CarPlay experience becomes available.

These requirements follow from the way the feature is built. Gemini Live is a voice-first mode, and the CarPlay implementation depends on the phone-side app having already established the user's voice profile and permissions. A driver who has never opened Gemini Live on the phone will not see the CarPlay option until that first phone session has taken place.

## Continuity between car and phone

Conversations held in the car do not remain in the car. They sync automatically with the Gemini app on the iPhone, so a discussion started while driving is available on the phone afterwards. Notes and summaries generated during a drive are waiting for the driver after parking.

This continuity is the practical core of the feature. A driver can ask Gemini to prepare a summary, draft a message, or work through an idea aloud, and then review the result on the phone once the journey has ended. The car becomes an extension of the assistant the user already carries, rather than a separate system with its own history.

## The last major chatbot to arrive

Gemini is the last of the major AI chatbots to reach CarPlay. ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Meta AI, Grok and Perplexity already offer CarPlay apps, and their presence has set the expectation that a voice assistant should be available on the dashboard. Google's arrival closes that gap, and it does so at a moment when in-car voice assistance is becoming a standard part of the driving experience rather than a novelty.

The timing also matters for Google's own product strategy. Gemini Live is the company's flagship conversational mode, and its value depends on being available in the places where users spend time. The car is one of the largest of those places: commutes and long drives are periods when a voice interface is the only practical way to use an assistant at all. A standalone CarPlay app puts Gemini in that space on equal terms with its competitors.

## Why it matters

The significance of the launch is structural rather than dramatic. No new capability was announced alongside it, and Gemini Live itself is unchanged. What changed is access: the assistant is now present on a platform where millions of iPhone users drive every day, in a form that requires no additional hardware and no separate subscription.

For drivers, the benefit is straightforward. A question that would otherwise wait until the end of a journey can be asked immediately, by voice, and the answer is preserved for later. For Google, the benefit is distribution. Gemini now competes directly with every other chatbot on the CarPlay home screen, in the environment where voice is the primary interface.

## What comes next

The rollout is still propagating, and users who do not yet see the Gemini icon on their CarPlay display can check that the Gemini app on their iPhone is up to date and that microphone permission is enabled. Google has not announced further CarPlay-specific features, and it has not indicated whether the app will gain additional capabilities beyond Gemini Live in the near term.

The broader question is how the in-car assistant market develops now that all the major chatbots are present. With the distribution gap closed, competition shifts to the quality of the voice experience itself: how accurately the assistant understands spoken requests in a noisy cabin, how reliably it completes multi-step tasks, and how useful its summaries are after the drive. Those are questions that will be answered by use, not by announcement.

Source: Google / Engadget

title: OpenAI turns ChatGPT into a storefront for businesses
body:
OpenAI has introduced a new commercial layer inside ChatGPT, allowing businesses to present themselves, their products and their customer support within the chatbot itself. The feature, named Businesses in ChatGPT, entered beta on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, according to OpenAI.

The launch marks a deliberate shift in the function of ChatGPT. A service that began as a general-purpose conversational assistant is now also a place where commercial entities can maintain a presence, be discovered by users and respond to customer enquiries. With 1.2 billion people using ChatGPT each week, according to OpenAI, the audience available to participating businesses is considerable.

## What launched

Businesses in ChatGPT comprises three connected elements: a verified business profile, aggregated performance insights and a labelled conversational agent known as a Business Agent.

A business can claim a verified profile through a new Business Hub inside ChatGPT. Once claimed, the profile allows the business to update its key details and to add self-service product feeds that include pricing and availability information. Any eligible business in a region where ChatGPT is available can claim a profile, according to OpenAI.

The second element is an insights dashboard. Businesses receive aggregated data on how often they are mentioned in ChatGPT, how many website clicks their presence generates and which topics lead users to discover them. OpenAI states that individual conversations are not shared with businesses. The data is therefore presented at the aggregate level, a distinction that matters for user privacy, since the conversations that produce the insights remain inaccessible to the businesses that benefit from them.

The third element is the Business Agent. This is a labelled artificial intelligence chat that operates inside ChatGPT and answers customer questions using the business's own product and policy information. OpenAI describes the agent as clearly separate from ChatGPT's independent answers, a separation intended to make clear when a response comes from the business rather than from the model itself. At launch, Business Agents are available only to eligible e-commerce and online-service businesses in the United States.

## What the agents cannot do

The limits placed on Business Agents are as significant as their capabilities. According to OpenAI, an agent cannot complete a purchase, take a booking or check the status of an order. A customer who wishes to carry out one of those actions must still be directed elsewhere, presumably to the business's own website or application.

This constraint defines the scope of the launch. Businesses in ChatGPT is, at this stage, a discovery and information channel rather than a transactional one. Users can learn about a business, examine its products and ask questions about its policies, but the completion of a commercial transaction remains outside the chatbot.

The limitation also shapes the competitive position of the feature. ChatGPT is not yet a marketplace in the full sense. Its value to a business lies in visibility and in the handling of routine enquiries, not in the closing of sales.

## Advertising enters the conversation

Businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent as a destination within ChatGPT Ads. Such placements are labelled, according to OpenAI, so that users can distinguish sponsored content from organic results.

The introduction of labelled advertising destinations inside the chatbot represents a further step in the commercialisation of ChatGPT. OpenAI has previously announced advertising in ChatGPT, and the ability to sponsor a Business Agent extends that model: a business can pay to place its conversational agent in front of users who are already engaged in related enquiries.

OpenAI did not state a price for claiming a business profile or for operating a Business Agent. The company also did not disclose the pricing structure for sponsored Business Agent destinations.

## Why this matters

The scale of ChatGPT's audience is the central fact behind this launch. With 1.2 billion weekly users, according to OpenAI, the chatbot is now one of the largest consumer surfaces on the internet. A business presence inside it offers access to users at the moment they are asking questions, rather than after they have navigated to a search engine or a marketplace.

For businesses, the appeal is twofold. First, the verified profile and product feeds create a structured presence that users can encounter during ordinary conversation. Second, the Business Agent can answer routine customer questions without human intervention, drawing on the business's own information rather than on the model's general knowledge.

For users, the change introduces a new distinction to observe. Responses from a Business Agent are labelled and separated from ChatGPT's independent answers, but both appear within the same interface. The clarity of that separation will determine whether users can readily tell when they are speaking with a business's representative rather than with the assistant itself.

The privacy arrangement also deserves attention. OpenAI states that businesses receive only aggregated insights and not individual conversations. That boundary, if maintained, limits the data available to businesses while still giving them a measure of how often they are mentioned and discovered.

## What comes next

The immediate questions concern expansion. Business Agents are currently limited to eligible e-commerce and online-service businesses in the United States, and the agents cannot yet complete transactions. Whether OpenAI extends the programme to other business categories, other countries and transactional functions will determine how far Businesses in ChatGPT develops beyond its beta form.

Also unresolved is the effect on the businesses that already depend on search engines and marketplaces for discovery. If a substantial share of product research migrates into conversational interfaces, the verified profile inside ChatGPT could become a standard part of a business's online presence, alongside its website and its listings on established platforms.

For now, the launch is a measured one: a beta programme, a limited initial category of businesses, and a clear set of capabilities and limits. Its significance lies less in what it does today than in the direction it indicates. OpenAI is positioning ChatGPT not only as a tool for answering questions, but as a place where commerce takes place.

Source: OpenAI / The Indian Express

title: TSMC bets $1B on Anthropic and OpenAI
body:
## TSMC bets $1B on Anthropic and OpenAI

TSMC, the world's biggest contract chipmaker, has approved investments of up to $1 billion in two of the artificial intelligence industry's most important companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, in a single board decision that ties the silicon supplier directly to the fortunes of its biggest customers.

The company's board of directors met on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, and approved an investment of up to $500 million in Anthropic, taking common shares at the AI startup's initial public offering price through a private placement, and up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock. The decisions were disclosed in a TSMC announcement and in a Form 6-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission dated November 10.

The two approvals together give TSMC a stake of up to $1 billion in the two labs whose demand for advanced chips has powered the company's record-breaking year.

## The Anthropic stake

Anthropic is in the middle of one of the largest technology listings in history. The company, best known for its Claude family of AI models, launched its IPO roadshow with an offering of 825 million shares priced at $70 to $78 per share, seeking to raise up to $64.35 billion.

TSMC's board approved an investment of up to $500 million in Anthropic common shares at the IPO per-share price, through a private placement. The structure means TSMC would become a shareholder alongside public-market investors at the same price set by the offering.

Anthropic's listing is closely watched across the tech industry. The company is one of the largest buyers of AI computing infrastructure, and its models compete directly with OpenAI's ChatGPT. The roadshow pricing range puts the offering among the biggest equity sales ever attempted by a private technology company.

## The OpenAI stake

The second half of the decision covers OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT and one of TSMC's most important indirect customers. TSMC's board approved an investment of up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock.

Together, the two approvals represent a deliberate bet by the chipmaker on the two AI labs that are driving the global build-out of AI data centres, the same data centres that are filled with chips manufactured in TSMC's fabs.

## The financial context

TSMC sits at the centre of the AI boom. It manufactures the most advanced processors used to train and run large AI models, including chips designed by Nvidia and custom silicon for the major cloud and AI companies. Every major AI lab is, directly or indirectly, one of its customers.

The investment decision is best understood against that backdrop. The company's October revenue was NT$586.89 billion, about $17.85 billion, a monthly record, up 59.7% year over year and 14.7% higher than September. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached NT$4.49 trillion, up 43.3% on the same period last year.

The company's third-quarter results were similarly strong: revenue of $45.50 billion and net income of $23.23 billion. At its October 15 investor conference, TSMC guided fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion.

The same November 10 board meeting that approved the Anthropic and OpenAI investments also approved approximately $40.93 billion in capital appropriations, the spending that funds new fabs and advanced manufacturing capacity, and up to $500 million to establish a strategic-investment company.

## Analysis: a circular flow of money

The structure has drawn attention in the industry because it creates a circular flow of money between the chipmaker and its customers. TSMC makes the chips that power Anthropic's and OpenAI's models; the two labs' spending on computing drives demand for TSMC's fabrication capacity; and TSMC is now using part of its profits to buy equity in both companies.

Analysts have noted that this kind of supplier-to-customer investment is unusual for a contract manufacturer, which normally keeps its distance from its clients' capital structures. But the AI boom has blurred the lines between chip supplier, cloud provider and model developer, and TSMC's decision suggests it wants a direct financial stake in the two companies most likely to keep ordering its most advanced chips.

The investments are also a signal of confidence. TSMC's board is approving the stakes at a moment when the AI industry's spending is under increasing scrutiny from investors, who are asking whether the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into data centres will produce commensurate returns. A $1 billion commitment from the company that builds the hardware is, in effect, a vote that the demand will continue.

## Status and outlook

Both investments are approvals, not completed transactions. The Anthropic stake is tied to the IPO price, so its final size will depend on where the offering prices within the $70 to $78 range. The OpenAI investment is in preferred stock, a structure that typically gives the investor a senior claim on dividends and liquidation proceeds.

TSMC did not disclose a timetable for completing either investment. The company will likely report progress in future filings, and investors will be watching whether the board's approvals are the start of a broader strategy of taking stakes in customers, or a one-off allocation to the two most prominent AI labs.

What is clear is that TSMC's record year is giving it the financial freedom to make moves few other chipmakers could contemplate. With monthly revenue at record levels, a fourth quarter guided at $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, and $40.93 billion in new capital appropriations approved in the same meeting, the company is spending on fabs, on strategic investments, and now on equity in the customers that keep its order books full.

Source: Taiwan News / The Hindu BusinessLine

title: CoreWeave revenue surges 168% to $3.66B
body:
## CoreWeave revenue surges 168% to $3.66B

CoreWeave just posted a quarter that shows both sides of the AI infrastructure boom: revenue nearly tripling, and losses widening just as fast.

The AI cloud provider reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $3.66 billion, precisely $3.661 billion, up 168% from $1.37 billion a year earlier. The result beat the roughly $3.55 billion analysts had expected, according to LSEG, and the market liked what it saw: shares jumped more than 16% in premarket trading on Wednesday, November 11, after rising about 7% in extended trading on Tuesday evening when the results were released.

## The growth figures

The headline figure is the growth. Revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168% year over year, is the kind of number that explains why CoreWeave has become one of the most closely watched names in the AI buildout. Demand for the GPU compute that trains and runs AI models is still surging, and CoreWeave, which rents out clusters of Nvidia chips to AI companies, is sitting directly in the flow of that spending.

The company also raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $13 billion and $13.3 billion, up from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. And its revenue backlog, contracted future revenue, hit a record $132.5 billion at the end of September, up from $104 billion at the end of June. That backlog is the clearest sign that customers are not just buying compute today, but locking in huge amounts of it for years ahead.

## The other side of the ledger

But the same report shows why the AI infrastructure business is not a simple growth story. CoreWeave's net loss widened to $709 million in the quarter, up from $110 million a year earlier. Net interest expense alone was $846 million, the cost of the enormous debt the company has taken on to buy GPUs and build data centres.

The spending does not stop there. CoreWeave plans $37 billion to $39 billion of capital expenditure in 2026, a staggering figure for a company of its size, and it is targeting adjusted profitability only in the first half of 2028. Total debt stands at roughly $46.9 billion.

That is the bet in a nutshell: borrow tens of billions, buy the chips, build the data centres, and trust that the AI demand, and the $132.5 billion backlog, will be there to pay it all back.

## Why the market cheered anyway

Investors focused on the growth, not the losses. A 168% revenue jump and a raised outlook, plus a backlog that grew by nearly $30 billion in a single quarter, suggest the demand side of the equation is holding up. The premarket surge of more than 16% is the market saying it believes the spending will pay off.

It is also a vote of confidence in the broader AI infrastructure trade. CoreWeave is a pure play on AI compute. It has no consumer business, no software franchise to fall back on. When its numbers beat, it is read as a signal about the whole sector's health.

## Why it matters

CoreWeave matters because it is a window into the economics of the AI boom. The company is building the physical foundation, the GPUs, the power, the cooling, that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic run on. Its backlog is, in effect, a measure of how much the AI industry expects to spend on compute in the coming years.

But the $709 million loss and the $46.9 billion debt load are a reminder that this foundation is being built on borrowed money. If AI demand keeps growing at anything like its current pace, the bet pays off handsomely. If it slows, the debt remains.

For now, the market is betting on growth. The 168% revenue surge and the record backlog say the AI buildout is still accelerating, and CoreWeave, for better or worse, is all in.

## What to watch

Watch the backlog number in the next quarter: if it keeps growing at this pace, the spending is justified in investors' eyes. Watch the path to the company's targeted adjusted profitability in the first half of 2028. And watch the debt. $46.9 billion is a lot of leverage to carry into a market that can turn quickly.

CoreWeave's quarter is the AI boom in miniature: extraordinary growth, extraordinary spending, and a share price that, for now, is rewarding the gamble.

Source: Reuters

title: Roku quits smart home to refocus on streaming
body:
## Roku quits smart home to refocus on streaming

Roku is getting out of the smart home business.

The streaming company confirmed on November 11 that it is winding down sales of its smart home hardware, ending a short-lived push into cameras, doorbells, lights and home monitoring that began only in 2022. The move is a sharp refocus on the business that made Roku a household name: streaming.

"We're sharpening our focus on Roku's core mission: being the top streaming platform… we plan to wind down sales of smart home hardware and will provide continued support and services for Roku Smart Home products," a Roku spokesperson told Lowpass, the tech newsletter run by Janko Roettgers that first reported the news.

## What is going away

Roku's smart home line covered video doorbells, indoor and outdoor cameras, smart lights, smart plugs and a home monitoring system. All of it is now being wound down.

The retreat is already visible on Roku's own web store. Only two smart home products remain listed, the Indoor Camera 360° and the Video Doorbell & Chime, and both are being sold at clearance, heavily discounted prices. On Amazon, the picture is similar: only refurbished Roku smart home models are still available.

What is not going away, at least for now, is support. Roku says it will keep supporting and servicing the smart home products it has already sold. The company has not announced any end-of-support date, so existing owners are not being cut off, but no new hardware is coming.

## A short-lived experiment

Roku's smart home push was never a long-term pillar of the company. It launched in October 2022, in partnership with Wyze, whose cameras and sensors Roku rebadged and sold under its own name, exclusively through Walmart at first.

The idea was straightforward: Roku already sat in millions of living rooms, and the TV was a natural hub for checking a doorbell camera or turning off a light. But the smart home market is crowded, margins are thin, and Roku's hardware was largely a rebadged version of products customers could already buy cheaper from Wyze itself.

Four years later, Roku has decided the experiment is over.

## The Fox question

The timing invites an obvious question. Fox completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku on November 6, just five days before the smart home exit was confirmed. Was the new owner behind the cut?

According to the reporting, no. The decision to exit smart home hardware was planned before the takeover closed, and the timing is coincidental. Fox bought Roku for its streaming platform and its advertising business, not for a sideline in doorbell cameras, but the call to wind the line down was Roku's own, made before the deal completed.

## The financial case

The financial case for the exit is easy to see. Roku's hardware losses more than doubled in the third quarter, widening from $22.9 million to $48.6 million. The company blamed the jump largely on rising memory-component costs, which have squeezed hardware margins across the industry.

For a company whose streaming platform and advertising business are its growth engines, a hardware line burning nearly $50 million in a quarter, and getting worse, was hard to justify. Exiting smart home lets Roku stop feeding a loss-making sideline and put the money back into streaming.

## A lawsuit in the background

The exit also comes with legal baggage. A class action filed in March 2026, Moses v. Roku Inc., Case No. 3:26-cv-01422 in California federal court, alleges that Roku removed the free Motion Snapshots feature from its smart home cameras in July 2025.

That is an allegation in a lawsuit, not an established fact, and it has not been proven in court. But it is part of the backdrop to the shutdown: a reminder that the smart home line generated not just losses but complaints.

## Why it matters

Roku's decision is a small story about one product line, and a bigger one about focus. The streaming wars have entered a phase where scale and advertising matter more than ever, and Roku, now part of Fox, is choosing to concentrate on the platform rather than spread itself across hardware categories where it had no real edge.

For existing Roku smart home owners, the immediate message is reassuring: your devices keep working, and Roku says support continues. The open question is for how long, since no end-of-support date has been given.

For the wider market, the lesson is familiar. A TV platform can sell a camera, but selling a camera is a different business from running a streaming platform, and when the losses doubled, Roku chose the business it actually knows.

## What comes next

Watch for clearance pricing to deepen as Roku clears remaining stock, and for the two surviving products, the Indoor Camera 360° and the Video Doorbell & Chime, to disappear from the store once inventory runs out. The bigger question is what Roku does with the freed-up focus: whether the Fox era brings new streaming moves, new advertising products, or a renewed push on the platform itself.

One thing is clear: the Roku smart home experiment is over.

Source: Engadget / The Desk

title: Apple is shutting down its 28-year-old support forum
body:
## Apple is shutting down its 28-year-old support forum

After 28 years, Apple's community support forum is closing for good. The Apple Support Community went read-only on November 10, 2026, and will permanently close on Friday, November 20, 2026, ending one of the longest-running user support spaces in tech.

For millions of Apple users, the forum was the first place to turn when a device misbehaved. Now they have ten days left to read it, and then it is gone.

## What happened

Apple posted a notice on the community site announcing the end. "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state."

The shutdown happened in two stages. On November 10, the site stopped accepting new posts, with the final post published at 5:49 p.m. PT that day. From then until November 20, the forum remains available to browse and search, but nobody can post, reply or start a new thread. On November 20, it closes permanently.

The change is already visible to anyone who tries to sign in. The sign-in link now routes to an internal AppleConnect employee login rather than a customer account, a clear sign the public community is being wound down. Users can still browse and search existing discussions, and the "Me too" and voting buttons on posts still work.

## 28 years of community support

The forum's history stretches back to the late 1990s. It launched in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange, a place where Mac users could help each other with problems Apple itself had not yet documented.

It was renamed Apple Discussions in 2000, became Apple Support Communities in 2011, and took its current name, Apple Support Community, in 2022. Across all those names, the model stayed the same: experienced users, many of them volunteers, answering questions from people stuck on a bug, a setting or a broken feature.

Over nearly three decades, the forum accumulated an enormous archive of troubleshooting knowledge, answers to problems that often never appeared in Apple's official documentation, from obscure macOS errors to iPhone battery quirks and iCloud sync failures.

## Why Apple is closing it

Apple's stated reason is brief. The company said the decision was made after "a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs."

The company has not elaborated further, and it has not said what will happen to the archive of old threads after November 20. Users who relied on the forum's search results may want to save the answers they need while the site is still readable.

The closure fits a broader shift in how Apple handles support. The company has been steering customers toward its official support channels, the Support app, Apple Support online, and in-store Genius Bar appointments, and toward its AI-driven support tools, rather than a public forum where answers come from fellow users.

## Why it matters

Community forums were once the backbone of tech support. Before chatbots and AI assistants, the fastest way to fix a strange error was often a forum thread where someone else had already hit the same problem and written down the fix.

Apple's forum was one of the oldest and largest of its kind, and its closure marks the end of an era in which companies hosted open communities where users helped users. For the volunteers who spent years answering questions there, some of them earning high community rankings for thousands of solved problems, it is the end of a community they helped build.

For everyday users, the practical effect is narrower but real: after November 20, one of the web's richest archives of Apple troubleshooting will no longer be open for new questions, and the peer-to-peer help that solved countless problems will need to find a new home.

## What comes next

The forum stays readable until November 20, so anyone with a bookmarked thread or an unsolved problem has a short window to use it. After that, Apple's official support channels, and the unofficial communities on Reddit, MacRumors forums and elsewhere, will absorb the questions that used to go to the Apple Support Community.

Whether Apple's own support tools can match the depth of 28 years of community knowledge is the open question. The forum's volunteers knew the obscure corners of Apple's software better than any manual, and that knowledge is hard to replace.

Source: MacRumors / 9to5Mac

title: United bans AI agents from booking your flights
body:
## United bans AI agents from booking your flights

United Airlines has drawn a hard line on AI in travel booking. In a revision to its Contract of Carriage dated November 11, 2026, the airline banned the use of AI agents to book, change or service tickets, one of the clearest moves yet by a major carrier against the new wave of agentic travel tools.

The ban is not a vague warning. It is written into the contract every United passenger agrees to, and it comes with a cancellation power attached.

## What the new rule says

The change arrives as a new provision, Rule 6.J.6, in United's Contract of Carriage. It bans "the use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product."

The scope is deliberately wide. The ban covers bookings made directly through united.com and the United app, and it also reaches agents working through travel agencies, aggregators or any other intermediary. Crucially, it applies even when the customer supervises or approves every step the agent takes. Human oversight does not make an AI-booked ticket acceptable under the new rule.

A companion provision, Rule 5.H, gives United the right to cancel reservations that were made, modified or serviced by AI agents. In other words, the airline can undo a booking it believes an agent touched.

## What is still allowed

The ban is about booking, not browsing. AI research and search are still allowed: an agent may show a traveller United flights and prices. The line is drawn at the purchase itself. The customer must complete the booking themselves.

There is also a grandfather clause. Bookings that AI agents made before November 11, 2026 will not be cancelled, so travellers who already used an agent to book are not about to lose their seats.

## Why United did it

United's stated reasons centre on security and control. Handing an AI agent your United login means sharing credentials, which the airline says exposes sensitive personal information. There is also the risk of unintended consequences: an agent acting on a traveller's behalf could make a purchase they did not mean to make, change account details, or spend MileagePlus miles without the traveller realising.

The airline also points to potential regulatory conflicts with the Federal Aviation Administration and the Department of Transportation, suggesting that letting autonomous agents transact on a passenger's behalf could collide with rules written for human travellers.

Chief executive Scott Kirby put the commercial logic more bluntly. "To be honest, I don't want to create another middleman," he told The Wall Street Journal, a reference to the industry's long fight over who controls the customer relationship, and the fees that come with it.

## Not everyone agrees

The industry is not united on the question. JetBlue president Marty St. George responded on November 12 at the Skift Commerce Summit, saying airlines should follow their customers' lead on AI booking agents, a signal that at least one rival sees agent-led booking as something to accommodate rather than block.

That split matters, because the technology is moving fast. AI agents that can search, compare and book travel are already being built into chatbots and assistants, and travellers are beginning to use them. United's bet is that the risks, security, unintended purchases, lost miles, outweigh the convenience for now.

## Why it matters

This is the first time a major US airline has written a ban on AI booking agents directly into its Contract of Carriage, with an explicit right to cancel offending reservations. It turns a question the industry has been debating in the abstract, should machines be allowed to buy tickets for people, into a concrete rule with consequences for passengers.

For travellers, the practical message is simple: you can still use AI to find your flight and compare prices, but when it is time to pay, you will need to do it yourself. For the companies building booking agents, United has just become the hardest airline to work with, and the clearest test case for whether other carriers follow.

## What to watch

Watch whether other major carriers copy United's language into their own contracts, or take JetBlue's position and lean into agent-led booking instead. The divide between the two approaches is now public, and the next few months will show which side the industry, and travellers, choose.

Source: View from the Wing / Reuters

title: NVIDIA board meets today to decide Huang's future
body:
## NVIDIA board meets today to decide Huang's future

Nvidia's board of directors meets today, Wednesday 12 November, to decide whether to remove chief executive Jensen Huang from the company he co-founded and has led for more than three decades.

The meeting comes days after reports that the board was preparing to oust the 63-year-old chief executive, and after a week in which Nvidia has lost around $600 billion in market value. Nvidia, worth roughly $4 trillion, did not comment.

## What the board is deciding

According to Reuters, the board is meeting today to decide whether to oust Huang. Bloomberg has reported that the board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements, and that an interim chief executive is under consideration.

No successor has been confirmed. Analyst Armina Rosenberg of Minotaur Capital described chief financial officer Colette Kress as the "natural choice", but that is an analyst's view, not a board decision, and Kress has not been named as a chosen replacement.

The succession question is central to the board's deliberations. Huang has no obvious successor, and he owns about 3.6% of Nvidia's stock, a stake that makes any decision about his future unusually complicated for the board. A chief executive who is also a major shareholder, and who has led the company since its founding, cannot be removed by the same straightforward process that applies to an appointed manager. The board must weigh the leadership question against the ownership structure, the market reaction, and the absence of a confirmed replacement.

## The market reaction

Shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading after The Wall Street Journal first reported that the board was preparing to oust Huang. Since the board announced its investigation earlier this week, roughly $600 billion of Nvidia's market value has been wiped out.

Monday alone brought a 4.3% fall in the shares, erasing around $190 billion, on the day a shareholder lawsuit was filed against the company. The scale of the decline reflects how closely investors associate Nvidia's value with Huang himself, and how much uncertainty the leadership question has introduced into a stock that had been valued at roughly $4 trillion.

## The lawsuit

A shareholder class action was filed on Monday 9 November in federal court in San Jose: Kistenmacher v. NVIDIA Corp. et al, brought by the Rosen Law Firm.

The suit alleges that investors were misled over reports concerning Huang's personal conduct and espionage-related claims. The class period runs from 9 October 2025 to 8 November 2026.

## What comes next

Two fixed dates now sit on the calendar. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on 17 November, numbers that will land while the leadership question is still open. The following day, 18 November, three House committees are due to hold a closed-door briefing on the matter.

US President Donald Trump has publicly backed Huang, calling him an "honorable guy" who has "done an amazing job", and said the FBI is "looking into it in terms of something else."

## Why it matters

Huang is not just Nvidia's chief executive. He is the public face of the artificial intelligence boom, and the architect of the company's rise to become the world's most valuable chipmaker. A board decision to remove him would be one of the most dramatic leadership changes in modern corporate history, and it would land at the exact moment the AI industry is asking how much of Nvidia's success is the company, and how much is the man.

Today's meeting will answer the first part of that question. The second part, who leads Nvidia next, and whether the company's $4 trillion valuation can hold without him, is only just beginning.

Source: Reuters

title: OpenAI's Cursor deadline is today
body:
## OpenAI's Cursor deadline is today

Today is the day OpenAI said it plans to cut Cursor off.

OpenAI has told SpaceX it intends to wind down the contract that supplies its models to Cursor, with a "proposed shutoff date of November 12, 2026", today. The deadline is proposed, not confirmed as live: as of November 11, the two companies were still talking, trying to resolve the dispute. But the clock OpenAI set has now run out, and Cursor users who rely on OpenAI models are waiting to see what actually happens when the day arrives.

## Background: the acquisition

OpenAI's decision follows SpaceX's acquisition of Anysphere, the company behind Cursor. SpaceX agreed in June 2026 to buy Anysphere for $60 billion in an all-stock deal, and the acquisition closed on August 14, 2026. Since then, Cursor has been a SpaceX-owned company, and OpenAI has decided it no longer wants to supply it.

## OpenAI's stated rationale

In a statement published on its official blog, OpenAI was blunt about why. "We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts."

That is unusually direct language from OpenAI, and it puts the dispute squarely in the open: this is not a technical disagreement or a pricing dispute. OpenAI says it does not trust that its technology would be used within the terms of the agreement once it is in the hands of a company owned by Elon Musk.

OpenAI also made clear the cutoff is not limited to the models Cursor uses today. The company said it will not provide future models to Cursor either, naming its upcoming model Astra among the models that will not be supplied. The door, in other words, is closing forward as well as backward.

## The scale of the impact

The practical impact may be smaller than the headlines suggest. Cursor CEO Michael Truell has said that OpenAI models serve only about 5% of Cursor's traffic. The overwhelming majority of what Cursor users run already comes from other model providers, and that traffic is unaffected by OpenAI's decision.

Truell also confirmed that the two companies are still talking to resolve the situation, even as the proposed deadline arrives. The fact that talks were ongoing as of November 11 leaves open the possibility of a last-minute agreement, or at least a delay. What is not in doubt is that OpenAI has set a date and said it intends to act on it.

## What stops working, and what does not

It is important to be precise about what ends if the shutoff goes ahead. What ends is the built-in, direct supply of OpenAI models inside Cursor, the models a user can select in the editor without any extra setup.

What does not end is everything else. Developers who bring their own OpenAI API key can keep using OpenAI models that way, and OpenAI's own IDE extensions keep working. The cutoff targets the direct commercial relationship between OpenAI and Cursor, not a developer's ability to use OpenAI's technology through their own key.
